Focused follow-up to two prior passes on the same project (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me, an agent pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites). The last pass found real, sourced material on WHAT signals a site is AI-generated/templated (Tailwind's own creator tracing the purple/indigo gradient to his bg-indigo-500 default; Kyle Chayka's New Yorker piece on Anthropic's Claude Design tool defaulting to the same cream/serif/terracotta look for every user; center-alignment, Inter font, and a 3-4 card icon grid all named as "safe choice" tells) but found almost nothing on the other half: concrete, actionable technique for HOW to deliberately break a design rule well. The only two sources found (Timothy Samara's "Making and Breaking the Grid" and the Interaction Design Foundation's rule-of-thirds page) are thin, print/photography-oriented, and neither explicitly connects rigid rule-following to reading as AI-generated or generic.

This pass has two goals. Use the same verification framing as the successful prior pass: "verified" means a named, identifiable source actually makes this specific observation, not that it is scientifically proven — Tier B named-practitioner opinion is the primary expected source type, refute a claim only when the cited source doesn't actually say it or is unsourced/anonymous content.

GOAL 1 — CONCRETE WEB-SPECIFIC RULE-BREAKING TECHNIQUE. Go deeper than the prior pass's thin coverage:
- Get more depth on Timothy Samara's named rule-breaking techniques specifically (split/splice/shift, spontaneous compositions, narrative constructs, working on an axis, intuitive design were named but not explained) — what does each one actually mean and how would it apply to a web layout specifically, not just print?
- Search for web-design-specific (not print-design, not photography) practitioner writing on deliberately breaking a grid, breaking alignment, breaking a type scale, or breaking whitespace conventions — real named designers or studios describing a specific technique they use, not a generic listicle.
- Is there a checkable HEURISTIC or TEST that a designer (or an AI agent generating a design) could apply to know whether they've broken a rule deliberately and legibly, versus randomly/illegibly? Precedent to look for: does any source frame it as "break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined" or "the violation only reads as a decision if everything around it is provably in order" or similar — a specific, named principle, not an invented one.
- Named case studies or portfolio critiques (Awwwards, CSS Design Awards, F5 Design Awards, The FWA, Godly, Land-book) where a juror or critic specifically praises a SPECIFIC rule violation (an element bleeding past the grid, an asymmetric composition, a broken type hierarchy) as the reason a design stands out. Try direct searches of those platforms' own blogs, interviews, and "site of the day" writeups rather than general web search.

GOAL 2 — TEST THE EMOTIONAL-VS-SYSTEMATIC HYPOTHESIS. The working thesis (from the person directing this research, not yet verified) is: AI-generated design results tend to converge on the same "safe" outputs because the generation process is fundamentally pattern-matching/statistical, whereas human designers break rules more often because they design from emotional/intuitive judgment rather than logical optimization — and that this is the core mechanism behind why AI output looks generic. Do NOT assume this is true. Search specifically for:
- Don Norman's "Emotional Design" and the "aesthetic-usability effect" (Kurosu & Kashimura's original 1995 study is the usual citation) — what does this research actually establish, and does it say anything relevant to deliberate imperfection or rule-breaking reading as more trustworthy/human, or is that a misapplication of a different finding (the aesthetic-usability effect is usually about attractive design being perceived as more usable, not about rule-breaking specifically — check precisely what it does and doesn't claim)?
- "Processing fluency" research in aesthetics/psychology — does disfluency (harder-to-process, less prototypical stimuli) ever read as MORE preferred or more "intentional" under any documented condition, or does fluency research actually point the opposite direction (fluent/prototypical is generally preferred)? This could refute rather than support the working hypothesis — report honestly either way.
- Any named design writing (not psychology research) specifically framing AI-generated design as "safe/optimizing/statistical" versus human design as "emotional/intuitive/risk-taking" as the explanation for generic AI output — search practitioner blogs, design critics, and design-education sources for this specific framing, distinct from Goal 1's "what are the tells" material already covered.
- Wabi-sabi / imperfection-in-design discourse as applied to digital/web design specifically (not the general aesthetic philosophy) — has any named practitioner written about deliberately designing in "flaws" or asymmetry as a countersignal to AI/template output specifically?

DELIVERABLE: same shape as the prior two passes — landscape with concrete named findings, confidence, and exact source. Explicitly flag: (a) claims with a real named source — usable; (b) the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis specifically — state plainly whether real sources support it, contradict it, or whether it remains an untested house theory with no source either way, since that distinction matters a lot for how confidently this can be written into doctrine. End with a short section proposing how any surviving Goal 1 findings could become an actual mechanism in the pipeline — a concrete gate, checklist item, or principle an agent could execute against (not just "be more creative"), the way the pipeline's existing "category-reflex check" (in loops/02-design.md: "if it's guessable from 'portfolio for a [category]' alone... throw it out") already gives a checkable test rather than a vague instruction.

result.summary: Goal 1 (web-specific rule-breaking technique) is now well-supported where the prior pass was thin: three independently named practitioner sources (Mohit Phogat, UsabilityGeek's Sean McGowan, Shiva Padival) each name concrete web grid-breaking techniques - overlapping elements, offset placement, irregular column widths, diagonal/rotated elements; containers, layering, whitespace, gutter/masonry effects - and converge on a competence-first heuristic: a deviation only reads as deliberate (not sloppy) if the designer first established the grid and can explain why every element sits where it does. However, the exact precedent the brief was hunting for ('break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined') was specifically searched for and REFUTED - the source that appeared to say it did not actually say it, so that precise framing should not be written into doctrine as sourced. Goal 2 (emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis) found no supporting evidence and one directly contradicting data point: the aesthetic-usability effect (Norman; Kurosu and Kashimura 1995) is narrowly about attractive designs being PERCEIVED as more usable, not about imperfection or rule-breaking reading as more trustworthy or human, and processing-fluency research is unidirectional - fluency, not disfluency, is what gets favorably evaluated, with zero documented condition where roughness or rule-breaking reads as more preferred or intentional. No named design-practitioner source was found this pass explicitly framing 'AI = statistical/safe' vs 'human = emotional/risk-taking' as the mechanism for generic AI output, no wabi-sabi-as-AI-countersignal source, and no Awwwards/FWA/CSS-Design-Awards juror commentary praising a specific rule violation - so the hypothesis remains an untested house theory (neither confirmed nor refuted), and two of Goal 1's specific sub-requests (named case-study praise, wabi-sabi discourse) came up empty rather than answered.

findings.claim: Timothy Samara's grid-breaking techniques remain named-but-unexplained even in the current (2023) 3rd edition, which added explicit but still-thin coverage of digital/UX/UI grid use.
findings.evidence: Google Books' catalog copy for the 3rd edition (2023) states 'Expanded discussion of grid use in interactive, UX/UI scenarios' (confirmed 3-0), extending the book's scope beyond print for the first time. But the publisher's own book-description page still only names the five techniques - split/splice/shift, spontaneous compositions, narrative constructs, working on an axis, intuitive design - with zero explanation of what any of them mean or how to execute them (confirmed 3-0), reconfirming exactly the gap the prior research pass flagged. A near-duplicate claim (citing a different Quarto URL) asserting the edition 'specifically expanded the book's scope beyond print to explicitly cover grid-breaking in digital/interactive contexts' was explicitly refuted 0-3 - so treat the digital-scope claim as resting on one confirmed source only, not two independent corroborations. Net effect for the pipeline: this book is still not a usable source of executable technique, digital or print.

findings.claim: The aesthetic-usability effect (Norman; Kurosu and Kashimura 1995) establishes that attractive designs are PERCEIVED as more usable - a perceptual bias, not evidence that attractiveness (or rule-breaking) makes a design actually more functional, trustworthy, or human-reading. No source in this cluster connects the effect to rule-breaking, imperfection, or disfluency.
findings.evidence: Kurosu and Kashimura's 1995 study (26 ATM UI variations, 252 participants) found aesthetic appeal correlated more strongly with PERCEIVED ease of use than with ACTUAL ease of use - confirmed identically by both NN/g and Wikipedia. Both sources were independently checked (keyword search of full text) and contain zero mentions of rule-breaking, imperfection, disfluency, or trustworthiness - this effect is strictly 'attractive = looks more usable,' not 'imperfect/broken = reads as more human or trustworthy.' Six separate verification passes across the two sources unanimously confirm this narrow scope, making this the best-corroborated finding in the whole research question and the clearest available evidence AGAINST casually citing the aesthetic-usability effect to support the working hypothesis.

findings.claim: Processing-fluency research directly cuts against the working hypothesis: fluency (ease of processing) is what's associated with favorable evaluation, one-directionally - no documented condition where disfluency/roughness is preferred, more interesting, or reads as more intentional/trustworthy.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia's processing-fluency article states 'Higher fluency is often associated with more favorable evaluations, even when the ease of processing is unrelated to the content itself.' A full-text check found no passage anywhere framing disfluency as preferred, more interesting, or more trustworthy/intentional - every example (product-form typicality, illusory-truth effect, mere-exposure effect) reinforces the same one-directional pattern. This is a single-source finding (session search budget was exhausted before cross-corroboration), but the check was deterministic (full-text grep of the primary artifact), and the honest reading is that this specific source contradicts, not supports, the hypothesis that AI-avoiding roughness/rule-breaking would read as more human via a disfluency mechanism. Note this does not rule out other disfluency literature (e.g., 'desirable difficulty' findings) existing elsewhere - only that this article doesn't document any.

findings.claim: Don Norman's Emotional Design argues attractive objects are perceived as more effective via visceral/sensual appeal - essentially Norman's version of the aesthetic-usability effect - and contains no claim connecting deliberate rule-breaking, imperfection, or disfluency to reading as more human, trustworthy, or intentional. This is negative evidence against using Norman as a citable source for the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia's summary confirms Norman's core argument verbatim ('aesthetically pleasing objects appear to the user to be more effective, by virtue of their sensual appeal') and his stated thesis ('technology should bring more to our lives than improved performance of tasks: it should be richness and enjoyment'). Two independent fetches, one specifically probing for imperfection/asymmetry/rule-breaking/disfluency content, found none - the book is about emotional connection and aesthetics improving perceived usability, not about norm violation as a design signal. This is a single tertiary source (Wikipedia summary of the book, not the book itself), so treat as indicative rather than exhaustive - but it is the closest 'obvious candidate' source for the hypothesis and it does not deliver.

findings.claim: Multiple named, web-specific grid-breaking techniques exist in current practitioner writing: overlapping elements past their column, offset placement, irregular/asymmetric column widths, diagonal/rotated elements (Phogat); and containers, careful layering, playing with whitespace, and gutter manipulation/masonry effect, each with a named real-site case study - Canatal, Cure Nails, Volta Footwear/NYT-Google Cloud, Randstad/Pinterest (UsabilityGeek/Sean McGowan). This directly answers Goal 1's request for web-specific (not print/photography) technique from real named designers.
findings.evidence: Both are dated 2026, named-author, web-specific practitioner blog posts (Tier B, the expected source type per this task's framing) verified by direct fetch of the live pages, with techniques matching the claims near-verbatim including sub-examples (e.g., 'a headline that starts at column 2 instead of column 1'; 'split-screen hero sections where one side is significantly larger'). Confidence is capped at medium per this task's own rubric because these are single blog sources per technique-set, not independently triangulated across multiple outlets, and Phogat's article cites two secondary sources ('Onething Design,' 'HypeEdge' 2025 analyses) that could not be independently verified as real publications - a mild reliability flag on that one article that doesn't invalidate the technique list itself (directly confirmed against the primary text) but should temper how much authority is assigned to it.

findings.claim: Convergent checkable heuristics for distinguishing deliberate rule-breaking from sloppy/random design exist across three sources: (a) the break must read as a decision, not a default - made by someone who understood the grid first (Phogat); (b) you must learn/understand the rules before you can break them, as a general precondition (UsabilityGeek); (c) breaking is a conscious act vs. ignoring which is unconscious, and the deviation only means something because the surrounding structure stays legible - operationalized as a specific test: 'can you explain why every element is where it is?' (Padival).
findings.evidence: All three quotes verified verbatim against live sources. This is the closest available match to the brief's hypothesized precedent ('the violation only reads as a decision if everything around it is provably in order') - Padival's framing in particular ('The grid remains present as the norm against which the deviation is read. The break means something because the structure it departs from is legible') is functionally the same idea, just not phrased as 'break exactly one rule.' Padival's two claims carry a lower-authority source (2-1 split votes; small-following Medium blogger, no stated design credentials, framing appears to be the author's own construction rather than traceable to an established grid theorist like Samara or Muller-Brockmann) - genuine Tier B opinion, not canonical theory, but it does meet this task's stated bar (named, not anonymous, actually says what's claimed).

findings.claim: Grid-breaking is explicitly context-dependent per practitioner writing: it works on portfolio sites, agency homepages, and marketing hero sections (exploratory-intent users) but fails on task-focused interfaces (e-commerce, dashboards, documentation) and when mobile is treated as an afterthought to a bold desktop design. This directly validates that the technique fits portfolio.me's product category specifically.
findings.evidence: Verified verbatim against the source: 'Broken grid layouts earn their place... when the product or brand benefits from feeling distinctive, and when users arrive with exploratory rather than task-focused intent,' naming portfolio sites, agency/creative-studio sites, and marketing landing pages as the 'works' case, versus e-commerce/dashboards/documentation as 'fails' because those need predictability. This is a single-source claim (medium confidence per rubric) but is directly on-point: it's independent confirmation, from web-design-specific practitioner writing, that portfolio.me's exact product category (personal portfolio sites) is squarely in the 'grid-breaking works here' bucket, not the 'grid-breaking fails here' bucket.

result.caveats:
Methodology note: because WebSearch budget ran out partway through verification, most confirmed claims rest on direct WebFetch confirmation that a named source actually says what's claimed, rather than triangulation across multiple independent sources - this matches the task's own stated bar ('verified' = a named source actually makes the observation, not scientific proof) but means breadth of corroboration is thinner than ideal for a few claims (flagged per-finding above).

Explicit refutations worth flagging by name: (1) The exact hypothesized precedent 'break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined' was searched for via a Studio Hoook Medium article and REFUTED 0-3 on two separate sub-claims - the source did not actually say this. Do not write this specific phrasing into doctrine as sourced; use the weaker but genuinely-sourced analogues instead (Phogat's 'decision vs default,' Padival's 'conscious vs unconscious' plus explainability test, UsabilityGeek's 'master the grid first'). (2) A Readymag blog post that seemed like an ideal source for 'build the grid first, then break it' was also refuted 0-3 on both sub-claims. (3) A near-duplicate Samara-edition claim citing Quarto's own retailer page was refuted 0-3, leaving the '2023 edition added UX/UI scope' claim resting on a single confirmed source (Google Books).

Unanswered (not negatively answered) sub-goals: Goal 1's request for named Awwwards/CSS Design Awards/FWA/Godly/Land-book juror or critic commentary specifically praising a rule violation returned nothing among the surviving claims - this needs a dedicated pass hitting those platforms' own blogs/interviews directly, which does not appear to have been attempted or at least did not survive verification. Goal 2's request for wabi-sabi/imperfection-in-digital-design discourse specifically framed as an AI-countersignal also returned nothing - same status. Neither is refuted; both are simply gaps in this pass's coverage.

Hypothesis status, stated plainly: the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis (AI = statistical/safe, human = emotional/risk-taking, explaining generic AI output) has NO supporting named source found across either research pass, and the one directly relevant strand of psychology research that was checked (processing fluency) points the opposite direction from what the hypothesis would predict. It should be treated in the pipeline as an unverified working theory, not doctrine, until/unless a design-critic or practitioner source is found making this specific framing explicitly.

Proposed pipeline mechanism (synthesis of the above, not itself a sourced claim - offered per the deliverable's request): a 'grid-break legibility gate' analogous to loops/02-design.md's category-reflex check. For every element in a generated layout that deviates from the established grid/alignment/type-scale/whitespace rhythm, the agent must be able to state, in the design rationale: (a) name the specific rule being broken (alignment point, column width, gutter, type-scale step, or spacing unit); (b) give a one-sentence non-generic reason for the deviation (emphasis, tension, narrative beat, brand voice - not 'to look less AI-generated'); and (c) confirm the same rule holds everywhere else in the layout except at that one deviation point. If (a)+(b)+(c) can't all be answered for a given element, revert it to the grid. This is directly sourced from three convergent findings above (Phogat's decision-vs-default test, UsabilityGeek's master-the-grid-first precondition, Padival's can-you-explain-every-placement test) and is checkable the same way the category-reflex check is checkable - it's a pass/fail question an agent can actually run against its own output, not a vague 'be bolder' instruction. Additionally, given the confirmed context-dependency finding, this gate should probably only fire for hero/landing/about-style exploratory sections of a portfolio site, not for any utility UI (contact forms, project detail navigation) the pipeline generates, since the sourced material explicitly says grid-breaking fails on task-focused interfaces.
openQuestions: Would a targeted pass directly on Awwwards/CSS Design Awards/FWA/Godly/Land-book's own blogs, 'site of the day' writeups, and juror interviews (rather than general web search) surface named critics praising a specific rule violation, as Goal 1 originally asked? This sub-goal was not answered by claims surviving verification in this pass.

Is there any named design-practitioner or design-critic source (distinct from the psychology literature checked here) that explicitly frames AI-generated design as 'safe/statistical' versus human design as 'emotional/risk-taking' as the mechanism for generic AI output? None was found across two research passes - worth one more targeted search before concluding it doesn't exist in citable form.

Does wabi-sabi or imperfection-in-design discourse, applied specifically to digital/web design (not general aesthetic philosophy), exist anywhere as a named practitioner argument for deliberate flaws as an AI-countersignal? Not found this pass; remains open.

Given that 'break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined' was specifically refuted as a sourced claim, is Padival's 'conscious act vs. unconscious act' plus explainability-test framing (2-1 vote, low-authority blogger) strong enough on its own to anchor a pipeline gate, or should the gate lean more heavily on the more solidly-sourced (3-0) Phogat and UsabilityGeek material even though their heuristics are less crisply testable?

refuted.claim: Samara's book (3rd ed.) names six specific techniques as methods for breaking a grid to create unique layouts: split/splice/shift, spontaneous compositions, narrative constructs, working on an axis, and intuitive design.
The 2023 third edition specifically expanded the book's scope beyond print to explicitly cover grid-breaking in digital/interactive contexts, i.e. UX/UI, not just editorial/print layout.

The article documents zero coverage of the aesthetic-usability effect, Kurosu & Kashimura (1995), Don Norman, design rule-breaking, imperfection-in-design, or AI-generated content — meaning this source cannot be cited as support for the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis in either direction; it is simply silent on it, and any claim linking processing-fluency research to deliberate imperfection reading as 'more human' would be an unsourced extrapolation not present in this text.

Readymag's own framing gives a checkable heuristic for legible rule-breaking: build a grid first for structure, then deliberately break it — precisely the 'discipline first, violate second' pattern the research question is looking for as a named principle rather than an invented one.

The same source states that a grid remains present underneath most 'post-grid' designs even when the visible result looks broken — i.e. the rule-breaking is layered on top of an intact underlying system, not a replacement for one.

The article's core actionable heuristic for legible rule-breaking is to limit a design to exactly ONE deliberate rule violation while executing everything else with discipline — the single violation reads as a strategic choice ('rebellion') precisely because everything surrounding it is consistent, which is what makes it feel intentional rather than accidental. This directly matches the precedent the research question was looking for ('break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined').

The article names the failure mode of breaking multiple rules at once ('do it everywhere') as producing 'noise, visual chaos that confuses rather than communicates' — offering a checkable anti-pattern (count the simultaneous violations; more than one signals illegible/random rather than deliberate breaking) rather than a vague 'be more creative' instruction.
